text: The first report made the incident look simple because it compressed three separate failures into one timeline. The sensor stopped updating, the alerting layer continued to display the last good value, and the handoff procedure assumed the display was live. None of those failures alone explains the delay. Together they created a believable false state. The fix is not a louder alarm. We need the system to represent freshness explicitly, make stale information visible at the point of use, and route uncertainty to the person who can act on it.

text: What matters here is not whether the model can produce an impressive answer once. A production system has to survive ordinary variation: longer sentences, interruptions, technical language, emotional pressure, and boring routine dialogue. Identity cannot disappear when the performance changes, and quality cannot depend on one lucky seed. So we test the voice the same way we would test any other persistent component. We hold the speaker constant, vary the conditions, measure what we can measure, and refuse to call a transient success a finished system.
